candidate.answerReason: Equidistance from the parallel tangents forces a point onto their midparallel, where its distance to each tangent is the radius. Exactly the center and two points twice the radius from the center also have that distance to the circumference.

methods.label: Midparallel and radial distance
methods.explanation:
Let the circle have center \(O\) and radius \(r>0\). Distance to the circle means the shortest distance to its circumference.

The two parallel tangents are each \(r\) from \(O\), on opposite sides, so their separation is \(2r\). Outside the strip between them, a point's distances to the tangents differ by \(2r\). Inside the strip, those distances add to \(2r\), so they are equal exactly on the parallel line halfway between the tangents. This middle line passes through \(O\), and every point on it has distance \(r\) from each tangent.

Now let \(P\) lie on the middle line and write \(d=OP\). Inside or on the circle, the shortest distance to the circumference is \(r-d\); outside, it is \(d-r\). These distances are attained along a radius: the triangle inequality prevents any other circle point from being closer. At \(P=O\), every circle point is distance \(r\) away.

For \(d\le r\), the equation \(r-d=r\) gives \(d=0\), yielding only \(O\). For \(d>r\), the equation \(d-r=r\) gives \(d=2r\), yielding one point in each direction along the middle line. All three points satisfy the conditions, and the cases cover every possibility. Thus the number is \(\boxed{3}\), choice \(\mathrm C\).
